questions.topic: while Loop — Sequential Increments and Condition
questions.q: What will this code snippet with a `while` loop output?
questions.hint: Think about when the postfix increment `i++` occurs relative to the `printf` call.
explanations: Correct! On the first iteration, `0` is output and `i` becomes 1. On the second, `1` is output (`i` becomes 2). On the third, `2` is output (`i` becomes 3). On the fourth, check `3 < 3` is false, and the loop terminates. Output: "012".
Incorrect. Postfix increment returns the value *before* increasing, so the first digit will be 0, not 1.
Incorrect. The loop will execute exactly 3 times (at `i = 0, 1, 2`); at `i = 3`, the condition becomes false.
Incorrect. Variable `i` increases on each iteration, so the exit condition is guaranteed to be reached.

questions.topic: while Loop — Infinite Loop
questions.q: What will happen when executing the given code?
questions.hint: Notice the absence of counter `i` modification inside the loop body.
options: The program will enter an infinite loop, continuously outputting character '0'
explanations: Correct! If you forget to update the control variable (increment `i++`), condition `i < 5` will always remain true, leading to an infinite loop.
Incorrect. The value of `i` never changes and remains equal to 0, so condition `i < 5` will never become false.
Incorrect. Syntactically the code is completely correct; this is a logical runtime error.
Incorrect. Since `i = 0`, condition `0 < 5` is true upon the very first loop entry.

questions.topic: do...while Loop — Guaranteed Body Execution
questions.q: What will this code snippet with a `do...while` construct output?
questions.hint: Recall the main difference of `do...while`: the loop body always executes AT LEAST once before checking the condition.
explanations: Correct! In `do...while`, the body executes at least 1 time. `printf` outputs 10, then `x` becomes 11. Check `11 < 5` returns false, and the loop terminates. Output: "10".
Incorrect. Unlike `while`, in `do...while` the condition is checked AFTER the first iteration, so output will occur.
Incorrect. Condition `x < 5` is checked after incrementing `x` to 11 and immediately stops the loop.
Incorrect. Syntax `do { ... } while(cond);` is written without errors.

questions.topic: for Loop — Empty Header Sections
questions.q: Is `for (;;)` permissible, and what will this code output?
questions.hint: Semicolons without expressions inside `for(;;)` create an infinite loop, from which exit is possible via `break`.
options: Syntax error due to empty sections in `for`
explanations: Correct! All three sections of `for` are optional. Construct `for(;;)` creates an infinite loop, but `if (i >= 3) break;` prematurely terminates it at `i = 3`. Output: "012".
Incorrect. Header `for(;;)` is completely legal in C.
Incorrect. Early exit from the loop is provided by the `break` statement.
Incorrect. At `i = 3`, `break` triggers before the `printf` call.

questions.topic: Loop Equivalence — Connection Between for and while
questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding the interchangeability of `for` and `while` loops is true?
questions.hint: Recall slide material: 'for = while in disguise'.
options: for and while loops are functionally equivalent: any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop, and vice versa
The for loop runs faster at hardware level than while
The while construct cannot be used if the iteration count is known in advance
The do...while loop is the only way to write iteration with a parameter
explanations: Correct! In C, `for` and `while` constructs are completely equivalent. `for(A; B; C) D;` fully corresponds to `A; while(B) { D; C; }` (except for `continue` statement specifics).
Incorrect. The compiler generates identical machine code for equivalent `for` and `while` loops.
Incorrect. `while` is perfectly suitable for a known iteration count (e.g. with an external counter `i++`).
Incorrect. `do...while` differs only in post-condition checking, not parameter support.

questions.topic: Loop Control — break and continue Statements
questions.q: What will the code snippet output when using `continue` and `break` together?
questions.hint: Trace the iterations: `continue` skips the rest of the body, while `break` instantly terminates the entire loop.
explanations: Correct! For `i=1` and `i=2`, '1' and '2' are printed. At `i=3`, `continue` triggers (printing is skipped). At `i=4`, '4' is printed. At `i=5`, `break` triggers (loop terminates). Final output: "124".
Incorrect. Value 3 is skipped due to calling `continue`.
Incorrect. Value 4 will also manage to print before `i` becomes 5.
Incorrect. Value 5 will not be printed because `break` terminates the loop prior to `printf`.

questions.topic: Loop Conditions — Postfix Decrement in Conditions
questions.q: What will this `while (i--)` loop output?
questions.hint: First value of `i` is evaluated for condition, then `i` decreases, and only then body executes.
explanations: Correct! 1) `i=3`: condition true (3), `i` becomes 2, prints 2. 2) `i=2`: condition true (2), `i` becomes 1, prints 1. 3) `i=1`: condition true (1), `i` becomes 0, prints 0. 4) `i=0`: condition false (0), loop terminates. Output: "210".
Incorrect. Inside loop body `i` is already decremented by 1 due to postfix decrement, so initial 3 is not printed.
Incorrect. The loop will make exactly 3 iterations, outputting 2, 1, and 0.
Incorrect. At `i=0`, condition check yields false and loop body does not execute.

questions.topic: Practical Tasks — Processing Sequence Until Terminating Zero
questions.q: Which loop construct is most natural for solving the task: 'Read numbers from keyboard and sum them until user enters 0'?
questions.hint: Refer to exercise list from presentation.
options: while or do...while loop checking that entered number is not zero
Fixed loop for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++)
Multiple duplicating copy-paste of scanf functions without using loops
explanations: Correct! In situations where iteration count is unknown in advance and depends on user input, `while` or `do...while` checking stop condition (zero input) is ideal.
Incorrect. We do not know in advance how many numbers user will enter — 5 or 500, so a fixed `for` with bound 100 is unsuitable.
Incorrect. Code duplication (copy-paste) is the worst solution.
Incorrect. In C there are no built-in exceptions (try-catch).

questions.topic: Comma Operator — Multiple Counters in for Loop
questions.q: What will this loop with multiple expressions in the `for` header output?
questions.hint: Trace changes in both variables: `i` grows by 1, and `j` decreases by 3 at each step.
explanations: Correct! Iteration 1: `i=0, j=10` (0<10), sum 10. Step: `i=1, j=7`. Iteration 2: `1<7`, sum 8. Step: `i=2, j=4`. Iteration 3: `2<4`, sum 6. Step: `i=3, j=1`. Iteration 4: `3<1` (false). Output: "10 8 6 ".
Incorrect. On third step `2 < 4` is still true, so third number 6 will also be output.
Incorrect. Variable `j` decreases by 3, not 1, so sums will decrease with step 2.
Incorrect. The loop will complete 3 iterations, not one.

questions.topic: Nested Loops — Modifying Outer Counter Inside Inner Loop
questions.q: What will the program output when modifying outer loop counter `i` inside inner loop?
questions.hint: Calculate how variable `i` changes in outer and inner loops.
explanations: Correct! 1) Outer `i=0`. Inner loop increases `i` by 2 (`i` becomes 2). Output: '2'. Outer step `i++` makes `i=3`. 2) Check `3 < 4` (true). Inner loop increases `i` by 2 (`i` becomes 5). Output: '5'. Outer step `i++` makes `i=6`. 3) Check `6 < 4` (false). End. Output: "25".
Incorrect. In second iteration `i` will increase from 3 to 5, not to 4.
Incorrect. Due to increments in inner loop, outer variable `i` grows much faster than standard step 1.
Incorrect. The loop will correctly terminate in 2 outer steps.

questions.topic: Practical Algorithms — Finding Maximum in a Sequence
questions.q: What common mistake is made when initializing variable `max` before loop finding maximum among $n$ input integers?
questions.hint: Think about what happens if user enters only negative numbers (e.g., -5, -10, -2).
options: Initializing max = 0, causing program to yield incorrect result (0) if all input numbers are strictly negative
Initializing max with first entered number of sequence
explanations: Correct! If initialized with `max = 0`, and input contains only negative numbers (e.g. -5, -20), condition `a > max` never succeeds, and program erroneously returns 0.
Incorrect. Initializing `max` with first element of sequence is actually a correct and safe approach.
Incorrect. Using `INT_MIN` is a correct solution for signed integers.
Incorrect. Using iteration counter is necessary for controlling loop step count.

questions.topic: Syntax Errors — Semicolon After while
questions.q: What effect will an accidental semicolon `;` immediately following `while (i < 3);` condition lead to?
questions.hint: Semicolon forms an empty loop body. Check whether `i` changes inside this empty body.
options: Program will hang in an infinite empty loop
explanations: Correct! Semicolon turns loop body into a null statement. Since `i = 0` does not change inside this empty loop, condition `0 < 3` remains true forever, and program hangs.
Incorrect. The block in curly braces below becomes regular block, but control never reaches it due to hanging on `;`.
Incorrect. No output will occur at all, as `printf` is located after infinite empty loop.
Incorrect. Null statement `;` is syntactically legal in C, so compiler will not issue an error.

questions.topic: do...while Syntax — Final Semicolon
questions.q: What is the syntax peculiarity of concluding a `do...while` loop compared to regular `while`?
questions.hint: Refer to syntax rules.
options: A semicolon is mandatory after closing parenthesis of condition while(condition);
Placing a semicolon at end of while(condition) is strictly forbidden
Body of do...while cannot consist of multiple statements
Using break or continue statements inside do...while is forbidden
explanations: Correct! Construct syntax strictly requires a trailing semicolon at end: `do { ... } while(cond);`.
Incorrect. Omitting semicolon at end of `do...while` leads to compilation error.
Incorrect. Body of `do...while` loop can contain any compound block `{ ... }`.
Incorrect. Loop control statements (`break`, `continue`) work fully inside `do...while`.

questions.topic: Unsigned Types — Risk of Underflow
questions.q: What will a loop with an `unsigned int` variable output when decremented down to zero?
questions.hint: Notice explicit `break` call at `i == 0`.
explanations: Correct! For `i=2`, `i=1`, and `i=0`, corresponding values are printed. When `i=0`, condition `if (i == 0) break;` triggers and loop terminates. Output: "2 1 0 ". (Without `break`, underflow to `UINT_MAX` and infinite loop would occur).
Incorrect. Iteration with `i = 0` manages to execute and print '0' before `break` triggers.
Incorrect. In this code an explicit `if (i == 0) break;` check is present, protecting against infinite loop.
Incorrect. Using `unsigned int` in loop header section is legal.

questions.topic: Scope — Loop Variables (C99)
questions.q: What will `printf` output after `for` loop completion if a variable with same name is declared inside loop?
questions.hint: Recall variable shadowing rules and scope of variables declared in `for`.
options: Compilation error due to re-declaration of `i`
explanations: Correct! Variable `int i = 0` declared in `for` header has scope restricted strictly to this loop. It shadows outer `i`. After loop completion, outer `i` remains 100. Output: "100".
Incorrect. Inner loop variable is destroyed upon exiting loop, without changing outer `i`.
Incorrect. Loop counter value is not transferred to outer variable.
Incorrect. Declaring variable in inner block/header with same name is completely legal in C99.

questions.topic: do...while Loop — Post-Condition Checking
questions.q: How many times will the body of this `do...while` loop execute?
questions.hint: Remember that `do...while` checks condition only AFTER executing loop body.
explanations: Incorrect. In do...while, body is guaranteed to execute at least 1 time before condition check.
Correct! Body executes 1 time: `x` becomes 1. Then condition `1 < 0` is checked — false, and loop terminates.
Incorrect. After first iteration `x = 1`, so check `1 < 0` stops loop.
Incorrect. Condition is false on first check.

questions.topic: Infinite Loops — Syntax Equivalence
questions.q: Are `while (1)` and `for (;;)` constructs functionally and performance-wise equivalent in C?
questions.hint: Consider whether generated machine code differs for these two options.
explanations: Correct! Both constructs create an infinite loop. C compilers translate them into identical machine code for unconditional jump.
Incorrect. There is no performance or behavior difference between them at compiled code level.

questions.topic: Nested Loops — Counting Total Iterations
questions.q: What will variable `count` equal after executing nested loops?
questions.hint: For nested loops, total inner loop iterations equal product of outer and inner loop iterations.
explanations: Incorrect. This is only outer loop iteration count.
Incorrect. This is only inner loop iteration count per single outer pass.
Incorrect. Nested loop iterations multiply, not add.
Correct! Outer loop executes 3 times (i = 0, 1, 2). At each step inner loop executes 4 times (j = 0, 1, 2, 3). Total: 3 * 4 = 12.
Incorrect. Outer loop runs 3 times, not 4.

questions.topic: continue Statement — Risk of Skipping Increment in while
questions.q: What will happen when executing this code with a `while` loop and `continue` statement?
questions.hint: Trace what happens to counter `i` when `continue` call transfers control directly to `while` condition.
options: Program will enter an infinite loop
explanations: Incorrect. Code will not reach completion due to infinite looping.
Correct! When `i` becomes 1, `continue` triggers. Control immediately jumps to checking condition `while (i < 3)`, skipping `i++`. Value of `i` forever remains 1, leading to an infinite loop.
Incorrect. Syntactically code is completely correct.

questions.topic: String Processing — Finding Terminator '\0' via while
questions.q: What will variable `len` equal after executing this string traversal loop?
questions.hint: Character array "C-lang" contains letters 'C', '-', 'l', 'a', 'n', 'g' and invisible null terminator '\0'.
explanations: Incorrect. Word "C-lang" length is 6 characters.
Correct! String "C-lang" consists of 6 visible characters. Loop increments `len` until encountering null barrier `\0`. Result: 6.
Incorrect. Null terminating byte `\0` terminates loop and does not increment counter.
Incorrect. First character 'C' does not equal `\0`, so loop starts running.

questions.topic: Compound Conditions — Logical AND (&&) in for Header
questions.q: What will `printf` print after loop completion?
questions.hint: Loop stops as soon as at least one part of condition `i < 5 && i != 3` becomes false.
explanations: Incorrect. Variable `i` manages to increment during first iterations.
Incorrect. At `i = 2`, conditions `2 < 5` and `2 != 3` are true, so step `i++` increments `i` to 3.
Correct! On iterations `i = 0, 1, 2`, both parts of condition are true. When `i` becomes equal to 3, check `i != 3` yields false. Loop terminates, and `printf` prints 3.
Incorrect. Loop will not reach 4 due to stopping at `i = 3`.
Incorrect. Condition `i != 3` terminates loop before reaching 5.
Incorrect. Counter increments at each step, no infinite loop.

questions.topic: Practical Algorithm — Sum of Number Digits
questions.q: What will value `sum` equal after splitting number in `while` loop?
questions.hint: Operation `% 10` yields last digit of number, while `/= 10` discards it.
explanations: Incorrect. This is only first extracted digit (3).
Incorrect. This is sum of first two digits (3 + 2).
Correct! Step 1: `123 % 10 = 3`, `sum` = 3, `n` = 12. Step 2: `12 % 10 = 2`, `sum` = 5, `n` = 1. Step 3: `1 % 10 = 1`, `sum` = 6, `n` = 0. Condition `n > 0` becomes false. Answer: 6.
Incorrect. Algorithm sums individual digits, not initial number itself.

questions.topic: Flag Variable — Early Exit on Condition
questions.q: What will index `i` equal after completing search for element with value 5?
questions.hint: Carefully check if `else` branch (containing `i++`) executes when match is found.
explanations: Correct! Element with value 5 is located at index 2 (`arr[2] == 5`). On this iteration branch `found = 1` executes, and `else` is skipped (index `i` remains 2). On next step `!found` yields 0, and loop terminates.
Incorrect. Since increment `i++` was in `else` branch, upon match `i` did not increment to 3.
Incorrect. Search terminates via `found` flag immediately upon detecting 5.

questions.topic: Edge Cases — Inexact Floating-Point Types (float/double)
questions.q: What is the critical danger of condition `x != 1.0` when working with `double` or `float` types in a loop?
questions.hint: Recall how floating-point numbers are stored in binary computer memory.
options: Due to rounding error, x may 'overshoot' exact value 1.0 and enter an infinite loop
This is a C compiler syntax error
The loop will never execute any iteration
Type double is forbidden to use in for loop headers
explanations: Correct! Fractional numbers (e.g. 0.2) cannot be represented exactly in binary. Accumulated error leads to `x` becoming e.g. 0.9999999999999999, then 1.1999999999999999, without matching `1.0` exactly.
Incorrect. Syntactically code is completely correct; this is a logical calculation precision error.
Incorrect. First iteration at `x = 0.0` will start without problems.
Incorrect. Floating-point variables can be used in `for`, but should be compared via inequality like `x < 1.0`, not strict `!=`.

questions.topic: Beginner Mistakes — Uninitialized Accumulator
questions.q: Does this code guarantee obtaining correct sum of numbers from 1 to 5 (i.e. 15)?
questions.hint: Check initial value of local variable `sum` before first addition.
options: No, because variable sum is not initialized to zero and contains garbage
Yes, in C all local variables are automatically initialized to zero
explanations: Correct! Local variables in C are NOT automatically zero-initialized. Variable `sum` contains residual memory value ('garbage'), to which `i` will be added, leading to unpredictable result.
Incorrect. In C, automatic local variables contain arbitrary garbage from memory unless explicitly initialized (`int sum = 0;`).

questions.topic: break Statement — Scope in Nested Loops
questions.q: What will variable `total` equal after code execution?
questions.hint: Remember that `break` statement terminates ONLY the single loop directly inside which it is located.
explanations: Incorrect. Outer loop will make 3 iterations.

Correct! Outer loop makes 3 iterations (`i = 0, 1, 2`). Inside on iteration `j = 0`, `total++` increments. On iteration `j = 1`, `break` triggers, exiting inner loop. Total: 1 operation per each of 3 outer passes = 3.
Incorrect. Inner loop terminates early at `j = 1`, without reaching `j = 2`.
Incorrect. Without `break`, result would be 9 (3 * 3).
Incorrect. Variable `total` definitely increments on first iteration of each loop.

questions.topic: Prefix Increment — Effect on Loop Condition
questions.q: What will variable `count` equal after completion of `while (++i < 3)` loop?
questions.hint: With prefix increment `++i`, variable increases BEFORE condition check.
explanations: Incorrect. The loop will make more than one iteration.

Correct! 1) `++i` makes `i = 1`. Check `1 < 3` (true), `count` becomes 1. 2) `++i` makes `i = 2`. Check `2 < 3` (true), `count` becomes 2. 3) `++i` makes `i = 3`. Check `3 < 3` (false), loop terminates. Output: 2.
Incorrect. On third step `i` becomes 3, and condition `3 < 3` stops loop.
Incorrect. The loop will complete exactly 2 iterations.

questions.topic: Array Bounds — Off-By-One Error
questions.q: What dangerous mistake is made in a loop traversing a 5-element array?
questions.hint: Recall index of last element in 5-element array.
options: Array index in C cannot start at 0
explanations: Correct! In C, elements of a 5-element array have indices from `0` to `4`. Condition `i <= 5` leads to attempted read of `arr[5]`, exceeding allocated memory bounds and causing Undefined Behavior.
Incorrect. Array indexing in C always starts at 0.
Incorrect. Loop syntax is correct.
Incorrect. Due to `<=` sign, loop attempts 6 iterations (for `i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5`).

questions.topic: Countdown — Counting Iterations from N to 0
questions.q: How many iterations will countdown loop `for (int i = 3; i >= 0; i--)` complete?
questions.hint: Do not forget iteration when `i` becomes strictly 0.
explanations: Incorrect. Iteration for `i = 0` was forgotten.
Correct! Loop executes for values `i = 3`, `i = 2`, `i = 1`, and `i = 0`. Since check sign is `>=`, value 0 is included in loop. Total: 4 iterations.
Incorrect. Values less than 0 (e.g. -1) will not pass `i >= 0` check.
Incorrect. Initial value `i = 3` satisfies condition `3 >= 0`.
Incorrect. Since `i` is signed `int`, it will normally become -1, condition breaks and no infinite loop occurs.
Incorrect. Loop will make 4 steps.

questions.topic: Nesting Control — Early Exit from Multiple Loops
questions.q: Which C construct allows instant exit from multiple deeply nested loops to a designated label?
questions.hint: Regular `break` exits only from one current loop.
explanations: Correct! Although `goto` is often scrutinized, exiting multi-nested loops to a label (e.g., `goto cleanup;`) is one of the few classic C tasks where using `goto` is justified by style guidelines.
Incorrect. In C, `break` does not accept numeric depth parameters (unlike languages such as PHP).
Incorrect. `continue` only transfers control to next iteration of the INNERMOST loop.
